big_idea: 2D shapes are FLAT. Circle, triangle, square, rectangle, hexagon. Each has a name and properties.
learning_intention: We are learning to identify and describe 2D shapes.
student_learning_goal: I can identify and describe 2D shapes.
success_criteria: I can describe a shape (round, sides, corners).
I can find 2D shapes in my classroom.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Sammy — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 1 shape tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Sammy spots a CIRCLE in the safari! What other 2D shapes can we find?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Sammy puppet. 'Friends — I'm Sammy the Safari Sloth. Today we hunt 2D shapes.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write 2D on chart. '2D shapes are FLAT — like paper.'

Show each shape one at a time. 'CIRCLE — round, no corners.' Hold up a circle card.
'TRIANGLE — 3 sides, 3 corners.' Triangle card.
'SQUARE — 4 equal sides, 4 corners.' Square.
'RECTANGLE — 4 sides, 2 long 2 short.' Rectangle.
'HEXAGON — 6 sides, 6 corners (like a snowflake).' Hexagon.

Describe each: rounded vs straight, sides, corners (vertices).

'Sammy hunts for these shapes everywhere. Window: rectangle. Plate: circle. Roof: triangle. Stop sign: hexagon (well, octagon really).'

Sammy's RULE: 'NAME IT — count SIDES — count CORNERS!' That's how Sammy hunts.

Class refrain. Class chants 3x with claps: 'NAME IT — count SIDES — count CORNERS! That's how Sammy hunts!'

'Today we identify and describe 2D shapes.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: identify 5 shapes by properties. Match name to card.
Three stations. Station A: Match shape to name. Station B: Sort shapes (round vs straight-sided). Station C: Find shapes in classroom (5+ each).
Stretch challenge at Station C: name a shape and find 3 examples.
Discuss properties. 'Sides, corners (vertices), straight or round.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Show shape anchor chart with names and counts.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the shape tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. 3 shapes only (circle, triangle, square).
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station C: 3 examples per shape AND describe each by its property (sides + corners).
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Sentence frame: 'A ___ has ___ sides and ___ corners.' Pre-teach each shape word with the matching hand gesture (circle = round hands; triangle = 3 fingers; square = box).
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-PAPER, NO-PURCHASE PATH: skip the 30 shape cards and the printed shape chart entirely. Children make shapes with their bodies — arms in a circle for CIRCLE; one child triangle (3 children hold hands in triangle); 4 children for SQUARE/RECTANGLE; 6 children for HEXAGON. Then they walk the classroom and POINT at things in the room (windows, doors, plates, books, clock face) and call out the shape name. Whole lesson runs on bodies + the existing classroom — no purchased shape cards needed.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: names 5 shapes; describes properties; finds classroom examples.

discussion_prompts: How do you tell a circle from a square?
consolidation.exit_routine: Refrain chant 3x. Then each child names ONE shape and ONE property: 'My ___ has ___ sides and ___ corners.' Sticky-note one shape and post on the Shape Safari poster.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 1 surfaces children who already grasp shape names vs those who confuse them.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child confuses square and rectangle — repairing the equal-sides distinction at K (van Hiele, 1986; Clements & Sarama, 2009; Clements, Wilson & Sarama, 2004)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A9.1 2D shape identification, the most-documented K trap is the square-rectangle confusion: child calls a rectangle a 'square' or vice versa. They have not yet differentiated shape names by PROPERTIES (sides, equal/unequal, corners) and instead operate on overall visual gestalt.

Van Hiele's (1986) levels of geometric thinking place K children at Level 0 (Visualization): shapes are recognised by overall appearance, not by attributes. Level 1 (Analysis) — recognising that a square has 4 EQUAL sides while a rectangle has 2 long and 2 short — is a developmental ACHIEVEMENT, not a starting state. The K target is to begin moving from Level 0 to Level 1: children identify by gestalt initially, then learn to verify by counting sides and checking equality.

Clements & Sarama (2009) trace this transition empirically: K children's most common error pattern is treating 'square' as a prototype label for any 4-sided shape (the prototype-effect). Showing tilted squares and elongated rectangles together is what dislodges the prototype. The 'shapes change when rotated' misconception below is a direct consequence of Level-0 visualization without Level-1 attribute analysis.

Clements, Wilson & Sarama (2004) on shape composition show that K children who can verbalise side-and-corner counts compose shapes more flexibly in later grades — making property-based identification a foundation skill, not a memorisation task.

Why this matters: a K child who exits with prototype-label-only shape identification will struggle through Grade 1-2 geometry, where rotational and class-inclusion reasoning becomes central. The repair is property-counting: every shape ID checks SIDES and CORNERS.

The walkthrough covers when child calls a rectangle a square.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. Shape card: rectangle. Child says 'square'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Let's check the sides. Are they all equal?' Run finger along sides. 'No — 2 long and 2 short. So it's a RECTANGLE.'

Walk through. 'A square has 4 EQUAL sides — all the same length. A rectangle has 2 long and 2 short.'

The child re-identifies. Generalise. 'Sammy says — count the sides AND check if they're equal. Square: equal. Rectangle: not equal.'

If still confused: provide ruler-strip. 'Measure each side. Equal? Square. Not equal? Rectangle.' Force the equal-side check.

Long-term recovery: every shape ID checks side equality.
expected_student_responses: (Stretched) Notices special properties (square is also a rectangle).
common_misconceptions: All 4-sided = square. (Repair: square has equal sides.)
Rectangle has only round corners. (Repair: 90° corners, like a square.)
Shapes change when rotated. (Repair: a square turned is still a square.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child uses 'square' as a prototype label for any 4-sided shape (Clements & Sarama 2009 prototype-effect): use ruler-strip to check equality of every side. Make the side-count + side-length-check explicit — 'Step 1: count sides. Step 2: are they EQUAL?' Repeat for the next 3 four-sided shapes. Tick 'describes properties' only when child applies both steps unprompted.

DIAGNOSTIC B — child says 'shapes change when rotated' (van Hiele Level-0 visualization, not yet Level-1 attribute analysis): rotate a paper square 45° to a 'diamond' position; ask 'is this STILL a square?'; physically count sides and corners with the child to show 4 equal sides and 4 right corners are unchanged. Generalise: 'turning doesn't change the SIDES or the CORNERS — those are the SAME.'

DIAGNOSTIC C — child names rectangles as 'long squares' (early class-inclusion confusion): show the side-equality check as a yes/no test: 'all 4 sides equal? YES = square. NO = rectangle.' Don't introduce class-inclusion ('a square is a special rectangle') at K — that's a Grade 2-3 move. K target: clean property-based labels.

parts_outline.task: Match shape pictures to names (5 shapes).
Sort 8 shapes into round vs straight-sided.
Find and draw 3 shapes from your classroom.
